newsitem.title: USA: McDonnell Douglas shelves long-range plane plan.
newsitem.headline: McDonnell Douglas shelves long-range plane plan.

text.p: McDonnell Douglas Corp. Monday scrapped plans to develop a long-range commercial jetliner that would have allowed the company to compete head to head with aerospace giants Boeing Co. and Airbus Industrie .
The St. Louis-based aerospace company attributed the decision to ground its MD-XX program to increasingly competitive pricing pressures for aircraft.
"We have decided that we are not going to proceed with the development of the proposed MD-XX airplane," said Tom Downey, a spokesman for McDonnell Douglas.

The project was regarded as the first step in a strategy that would have put McDonnell Douglas in direct competition with Boeing and the European Airbus consortium as a fully fledged commercial airplane manufacturer.

"The combined investment isn't merited right now when you weigh it against the risk that is involved in making it a financial and market sucess," Downey said. "There is a lot of intensity in the climate of pricing out there right now."
McDonnell Douglas has been working on the plans for about six months.

The project worked on two versions of the MD-XX. One model had a seating capacity of about 300 passengers, like the MD-11, the company's current longest-range aircraft. But it would have had a 20 percent greater range, allowing it to fly about 9,775 miles.
The second "stretch" version was 31 feet longer than the MD-11 and could seat 375 passengers.

The plane would have have been positioned against Boeing's 777 aircraft and the Airbus a330/340. The current 777-200 model seats from 305-328 in typical three-class configuration and has a range of 4,350-8,320 miles, depending on weight. Boeing also plans 777-100 and -300 versions with longer range and more capacity.

The MD-XX would have required a new wing, which analysts said would have cost about $2 billion to develop, with another $1 billion needed for infrastructure upgrades at the company's Douglas Aircraft unit to build the jetliner.
Analysts said the aerospace giant had netted about 50 orders for the MD-XX.
The move was preceded on Friday by the resignation of the head of McDonnell Douglas's aerospace business, Herbert Lanese, who left the company after clashing with Chief Executive Harry Stonecipher.
Downey said McDonnell Douglas will focus on its niche market of 100-150 seat airplanes, as well as cargo freighters.
Word of the decision to drop the MD-XX was first reported Monday by the Wall Street Journal.
The company held a conference call Monday with industry analysts to discuss its outlook in light of the unexpected announcement.
"They're definitely pulling in their horns in terms of expansion," said one analyst, who asked not be identified.

"It would be real tough for Douglas to broaden out their product line," he said. "They think they have a strong position in certain niches, but the investment needed to be a stronger player would be too onerous."
While McDonnell-Douglas has shelved plans to compete in the long-range, high-seating aircraft category, it will now refocus its efforts on smaller planes.
"We're evaluating alternate strategies to ensure our long-term success in the market," Downey said.

Analysts said McDonnell balked at the investment needed to develop the range of aircraft it would need to compete head-on with Boeing and Airbus in the commercial airplane market. McDonnell would have had to spend up to $15 billion over 10-15 years, they said.
McDonnell may dust off its plans for the MD-XX if a suitable partner can be found that will share the burden of the investment, experts said.
"They will be looking for partners that would like to make major investments into (Douglas Aircraft)," said Paul Nisbet, of JSA Research Inc.
"If they get that, they could change their picture. But they're not going to go it alone because of the tremendous investment involved," Nisbet said.
Some analysts speculated that McDonnell Douglas may choose to sell Douglas Aircraft, saying that Stonecipher would be ammenable to the idea if the price were right.
"I do recall Stonecipher ... saying 'If you can find a buyer willing to spend a premium price for commercial operations, give me a ring, immediately,'" said Nisbet.
But he added, "It probably isn't very saleable."
McDonnell Douglas' stock lost $1.125 to end at $52 on the New York Stock Exchange.
